neighbours.label: Expository present-tense advice weighing approaches: the evaluative word in 'the easiest/most effective way', 'the really neat thing', or 'This can/could …' and ', but' resuming the previous general statement (the − pole takes counterfactual 'would')
fire: There are many ways to back up your photos. You can copy them to an external drive every week. This method is cheap, but it is easy to forget. The simplest way to stay safe is to use an automatic cloud service. This can protect you even if your laptop is stolen.
Gardeners often water their plants at noon. This can waste a lot of water through evaporation. The most effective way to water is early in the morning, but few people get up in time.
Some teams write all their tests at the end of a project. This approach saves time at first, but it hides bugs for months. The best way to avoid this is to write tests as you go.
Many runners skip the warm-up before a race. This can lead to pulled muscles and slow starts. The easiest way to prevent injury is to jog lightly for ten minutes.
You can store passwords in a notebook or in your browser. This is convenient, but it is not very secure. The really nice thing about a password manager is that it remembers everything for you.
Most beginners learn chords by memorising charts. This works for a while, but it limits what you can play. The quickest way to improve is to learn how chords are built.
Bread dough can be kneaded by hand or in a mixer. This choice affects the texture, but not the flavour. The most reliable way to judge the dough is to stretch a small piece.
Small shops often track their stock on paper. This can cause errors when sales are busy. The simplest way to fix the problem is to use a barcode scanner.
quiet: Last summer we backed up our photos before the trip. My brother copied them to an external drive on Friday. He packed the drive in his bag and forgot about it. We found the bag in the car on Sunday. Nobody had touched the laptop.
My grandfather watered his plants at noon every day. He carried the water from the well in two buckets. One morning he got up early and walked to the market instead.
Our team wrote all the tests at the end of the project. Maria fixed the last bug in March. Then we shipped the release and went out for dinner.
Yesterday the runners skipped the warm-up before the race. Tom pulled a muscle on the second lap. He jogged slowly back to the tent and sat down.
She kept her passwords in a notebook in the kitchen. One evening the notebook fell behind the stove. Her son found it there a month later.
As a boy he learned chords from an old chart on the wall. His uncle played the guitar at weddings. They practised together every Sunday afternoon.
My aunt kneaded the bread dough by hand that morning. She put it near the window and went shopping. The loaf was ready when the guests arrived.
The old shop tracked its stock in a paper ledger. The owner counted the boxes every Friday night. In 1998 he sold the shop and moved to the coast.

notes: Card: ' This'/' that'/' but'/' way' in explanatory how-to prose; − pole is hypothetical ' would' and its logits suppress would/could. Probes: single sentences 0.05-0.11; a five-sentence how-to passage 0.39 on ' easiest', 0.20 on 'This could'; narrative past 0.004-0.02. Needs several sentences of expository context.
